title: “How Do You Do It All?”
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to the question of how he manages teaching, writing, speaking, and family, Dave Stuart Jr. answers that he does not do it all and describes what he leaves undone. He no longer hunts online for lesson ideas, instead asking what the best path to student mastery is and reflecting afterward. He deliberately does not grade everything to the maximum, separates grading from feedback, and favors speed and helpfulness in responding to writing. He plans lessons the morning of, anchored by pre-set unit dates and unit-long reading assignments, and holds no leadership roles at school because he found he could not be both a writer for teachers and a committee lead. The through-line is that deciding what to drop is the hardest and most important time-management discipline.
points: The honest answer to doing it all is subtraction: he skips lesson-plan hunting, maximal grading, long-range planning, and school leadership roles.
Years of reading and practice with a simple framework let him plan a day's lessons in the morning with a basic structure of texts and discussion methods.
Grading and feedback are not the same thing, and students benefit most from fast, helpful responses rather than long comments or elaborate rubrics.
Setting unit dates and distributing a unit's reading homework in advance makes lightweight daily planning resilient to disruptions.
Declining committee and department leadership was a necessary trade after trying and failing to be both a national writer and an internal leader.
quotes: I can’t remember the last time I went online looking for a lesson plan idea. Instead of trying to find something to teach a certain skill, I just sit and ask myself, “What’s the best path to getting my students to understanding X or mastering Y?” And then I do what I think will work, and afterwards I reflect on whether or not it did.

I never grade things as best I can. There are very few things that I maximize my efforts on, and grading is not one of them. First of all, grading isn’t the same thing as feedback, and sometimes you don’t need to do either. When it comes to giving feedback on student writing, I’ve learned that speed and helpfulness are qualities students care about and grow from the most — not the length of my comments or the complexity of my rubrics.

This means that I am typically prepping the day’s lessons in the morning before school starts. At this point I’ve used These 6 Things for so many years that the prep is very basic — what text(s) will we be reading, what discussion method would I like to use (Think-Pair-Share, Conversation Challenge, or Pop-Up Debate), that sort of thing.

The reason I don’t plan further ahead is because 1) I don’t have time with all the writing I have to get done and 2) this system has worked so well the past few years that I see no reason to change it. It’s remarkably efficient and it can’t get messed up very easily by disruptions because the disruptions have to come on the same day in which I’m doing the planning.

The trouble is that I can’t be both a writer for teachers around the world and a teacher and a PLC or department or committee leader. I tried; it didn’t work. This is why the most important (and hardest) discipline of time management tends to be deciding.
